name: Teddy Boy cut

card.summary: The 1950s British greased quiff with swept-back sides meeting in a ducktail, worn for a bold retro silhouette that adds height and shape on top.
card.note: Needs length on top and heavy styling product; strongly tied to the Teddy Boy subculture.

quick.overview:
The Teddy Boy cut is the classic 1950s British working-class youth hairstyle: long, greased hair moulded into a high quiff at the front, with the sides combed back to meet at the rear in a shape called the duck's arse (DA). It adds volume above the forehead and a strong, sculpted profile.

It grew out of the Teddy Boy subculture, which mixed Edwardian dandy tailoring with American influences, and it returned in the 1970s revival with larger pompadours and long sideburns. Today it is a retro choice within quiff and pompadour styling.
quick.how: The look needs hair long enough to sweep up and back. Wearers traditionally used grease or pomade to hold the shape, and revivalists in the 1970s added hairspray. Sides are combed back to meet at the rear, and sideburns are often kept long.
quick.risks: No health risks are documented beyond those of heavy styling products on hair and scalp. Socially, the style carries the strong subculture identity of the Teddy Boys, a group associated in the 1950s with gang violence and, in 1958, the Notting Hill riots.

lead: The Teddy Boy cut is a men's hairstyle from 1950s Britain, defined by long, heavily moulded and greased hair with a quiff at the front and the sides combed back to meet at the rear in a ducktail, known as the duck's arse or DA.[1] A related variant, the Boston, was greased straight back and cut square across the nape.[1]

The style adds height and a sculpted outline to the head, which is how people use it: a tall front section frames the forehead and lengthens the face. The quiff combines elements of the 1950s pompadour and the flattop and arose as a post-war reaction to short, strict men's haircuts.[2]

The look emerged around 1952 among suburban working-class youth in London and spread across Britain; the name Teddy Boy entered common use after a 1953 Daily Express article.[1] A 1970s revival, promoted by Vivienne Westwood and Malcolm McLaren's shop Let it Rock, brought flamboyant pompadours and long sideburns.[1]

angle.text: The cut is a styling choice that stacks volume above the forehead and sweeps the sides back, giving a taller, more dramatic head shape. Wearers pair it with long sideburns and period clothing.

infobox: Grease or pomade; hairspray in the revival

paras: The classic version is long, greased hair with a pronounced quiff and sides combed back to meet in the rear.[1] The revival pompadour of the 1970s was more flamboyant and accompanied long sideburns.[1] The modern quiff keeps longer hair at the front, tapering to trimmed sides and back.[2]

The Teddy Boy style appeared around 1952 among suburban working-class youth in London and then across Britain, drawing on Edwardian dandy fashion and American zoot suits and tied to rock and roll and a rejection of postwar austerity.[1] The name came into official use after a 1953 Daily Express article.[1]

Revivals followed: Westwood and McLaren's Let it Rock shop promoted the look in the 1970s, and revivalists returned to the 1950s version in the late 1980s and early 1990s.[1] The quiff itself returned in Europe in the early 1980s and resurged in the 1990s.[2]
The subculture became associated with gang violence, including the 1958 Notting Hill race riots.[1] The word quiff has an uncertain etymology, with suggested roots in French coiffe or Dutch kuif.[2]
